svg.font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, Segoe UI, Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: One detent of the rotary encoder, and the bounce it arrives with
svg.desc: Two pin traces, CLK and DT, a quarter cycle apart. Both rest high; CLK falls, then DT, then CLK rises, then DT, and only that last transition back to rest emits a step. Every edge carries a burst of contact bounce that the state machine absorbs.
svg.text: One detent, and the bounce it arrives with
Rest is both pins high. A complete cycle is one click; anything that does not complete one emits nothing at all.
CLK
DT
rest
rest again
+1, here and nowhere else
the only transition in the whole
table that emits a clockwise step
the chatter on every edge is contact bounce: twenty clicks gave 453 edges, and 88 of them survived a 1 ms debounce
none of which the decoder is told about - a partial transition routes back to rest, so bounce advances nothing
why this is bounce-proof rather
than bounce-tolerant
Every row of the table covers all
four pin combinations, so nothing
can fall through. A transition that
does not belong to the direction
being tracked routes back to rest.
Sampling the partner pin at an edge
is the classic approach, and it reads
bounce as direction: during a bounce
the partner is whatever it happens
to be.
Anticlockwise is the mirror image:
DT falls first.
Which way counts as forwards cannot be derived - it depends on which pin was called CLK when the module was wired - so it was
settled by turning the real knob. What crosses to the render loop is not this waveform but an integer: the callback thread adds to it
under a lock, and the loop takes the whole balance once a frame. Only counts survive between frames, never the order of events.
